Procurement — action required

○
UMLS API key
Free from uts.nlm.nih.gov — register with institutional email. Required before P1 and P2 pipelines can run. Approval is instant for academic institutions. Also download the current UMLS Metathesaurus release (UMLS Full Release, ~5GB zipped).
○
Neo4j Aura Professional account
Create at neo4j.io/cloud. For development: Aura Free tier works (but 200K node limit — switch before seeding full SNOMED). Production: AuraDB Professional ($65/month). Select us-east-1 to match Supabase region for lower latency writes.
○
Supabase project
Create two projects at supabase.com: journey-production and journey-staging. Enable pgvector extension, Supabase Pooler (Supavisor), and Point-in-Time Recovery on both. Enable Realtime for the lectures and mastery_snapshots tables.
○
Anthropic API key
Apply for production API access at console.anthropic.com. Request increased rate limits for Sonnet 4 (generation pipeline) and Haiku 4.5 (classification + enrichment). Medical education generation can hit 100K tokens/minute during batch generation — confirm limits before first faculty demo.
○
Hetionet data
Download from github.com/hetio/hetionet — hetionet-v1.0-edges.sif.gz and hetionet-v1.0-nodes.tsv (~60MB). Load into a Supabase schema named hetionet using the provided import scripts. No license required — CC0 public domain.
○
DrugBank academic license
Apply at drugbank.ca/releases/latest — Academic license is free for non-commercial use at accredited institutions. Download XML (~1.5GB). Required for drug mechanism enrichment in P2. Processing: 2-3 days for approval.
○
MedCPT model
Download from huggingface.co/ncats/MedCPT-Query-Encoder. Set up inference endpoint on Railway or Fly.io (Python, ~500MB model). Or use Replicate: ncats/medcpt. Needed before P1 embedding step. Test with a medical text query before connecting to pipeline.
○
Inngest account
Create at inngest.com. Start with the free tier for development (50K function runs/month). Production: Team plan (~$50/month) for concurrent function limits and 7-day log retention. Configure event signing keys for P1, P2, P3 and the weekly crons.

Codebase setup — first day

○
Repository structure
apps/web (Next.js 15), apps/inngest (pipeline functions), packages/db (Supabase client + migrations), packages/neo4j (driver + query wrapper), packages/ai (Anthropic client + prompts), packages/embeddings (MedCPT + OpenAI), scripts/seeds (all 14 seed scripts in execution order). Monorepo with turbo.
○
.env.example from tech arch §VIII
All 30+ environment variables are defined in the tech architecture document Infrastructure section. Copy them into .env.example and share with the team through your secrets manager (Doppler or Vercel environment variables). Never commit actual keys.
!
MetaMap setup is slow — start early
MetaMap (Java NLP service) requires a local installation or a Dockerized sidecar. The setup takes 4-6 hours including downloading the UMLS data files it depends on. This is the most painful dependency. Alternative for early development: use the UMLS API directly (slower but no local setup) and swap to MetaMap before production. Do this in Week 1.
!
SAML/SSO configuration requires MSM IT coordination
Shibboleth configuration requires MSM's IT department to register Journey OS as a Service Provider in their Identity Provider. This can take 2-4 weeks for approvals. Start this conversation in Week 1 even if the feature isn't needed until Week 8. Required before any real faculty or student accounts can be created.

IV / Competitive Moats

What makes this hard to replicate — the 8 defensible advantages

These are not features. Features can be copied in a sprint. These are compounding structural advantages — each one is harder to replicate the longer Journey OS operates, because they improve with data and use.

Moat 01 — Knowledge Graph
The curriculum as a graph — not a database
Once MSM's 22 courses are in the graph, the system knows: which concepts are taught together, which concepts precede others, which concepts have the most downstream dependencies, and which concepts are never assessed. This is a proprietary enriched medical knowledge graph for one institution's curriculum. Competitors who store items in relational databases can never ask "what concepts does this lecture teach that no exam currently covers?" Journey OS answers this in a single Cypher query.
SubConcept (77K+ nodes at full MSM) · TEACHES edges with evidence grades · LOD-verified via UMLS + Hetionet · Compounds over time — more lectures = richer graph
Moat 02 — Provenance Chain
Every item traces to a slide
SOURCED_FROM edge: AssessmentItem → ContentChunk → LectureSection → Lecture → CatalogCourse. The complete provenance chain is traversable. A faculty member can ask "which lecture slide did this question come from?" and get the exact slide number. This is the LCME validity argument: assessment items are demonstrably grounded in curriculum content. No competitor can make this claim because no competitor stores this chain. It's also a legal defense: if a student challenges an item, faculty can show exactly what curriculum content supports it.
SOURCED_FROM · HAS_CHUNK · HAS_SECTION edges · source_chunk_uuids[] on every item · Toulmin chain includes lecture citation
Moat 03 — ECD-Grounded Generation
Defensible assessments, not just questions
Every item has a validity argument before it's written: ProficiencyVariable (what mastery means), evidence rules (what correct selection proves), TaskShell selection (what situation elicits evidence), MisconceptionCategory-grounded distractors (what wrong selection reveals). The Toulmin chain stores the full argument. Competitors generate questions from prompts. Journey OS generates measurement instruments grounded in 50 years of assessment science (Mislevy ECD, Kane validity, Haladyna 22 rules). An LCME reviewer who asks "how do you know these items are valid?" gets a documented answer. Competitors don't have that answer.
ProficiencyVariable · TaskShell · MisconceptionCategory · Toulmin JSONB · Evidence rules per distractor · CLAIMS_ABOUT → ProficiencyVariable
Moat 04 — Self-Improving Distractor Loop
Distractors get better with every wrong answer
When a student selects the wrong answer, the Attempt record updates MisconceptionCategory.empirical_frequency. The next time P3 generates a distractor for that USMLE system, it queries misconceptions ordered by empirical_frequency DESC — the most commonly confused concepts become the most likely distractors. The item bank self-calibrates. After one academic year, the misconception frequency data reflects the actual cognitive errors of MSM students specifically — not generic medical student population norms. This is proprietary data that makes the assessment increasingly precise for MSM students over time.
TARGETS_MISCONCEPTION · MisconceptionCategory.empirical_frequency · BKT slip detection · Distractor selection query ordered by empirical frequency
Moat 05 — LOD-Enriched Context
Generation grounded in real medical ontologies, not LLM memory
Every generated item has access to a 200-token LOD brief assembled from UMLS + Hetionet + DrugBank + MeSH at generation time. The LLM doesn't need to remember drug mechanisms — it has the current authoritative data. Competitors using direct LLM prompting generate from training data that may be years out of date. Journey OS can generate items about a drug approved in 2025 with accurate mechanism data the moment the DrugBank release is updated. The knowledge base is maintained, not baked into model weights.
subconcept_lod_briefs Supabase table · LOD brief always included in generation context (D10) · Quarterly expiry and regen · UMLS, Hetionet, DrugBank, MeSH sourced
Moat 06 — LCME Accreditation Evidence Chain
LCME compliance evidence generated automatically
COVERS_LCME_DOMAIN edges mean every ContentChunk is classified against LCME Standards 7.1–7.9. The coverage chain: CatalogCourse → Lecture → ContentChunk -[COVERS_LCME_DOMAIN]→ LCMEContentDomain → LCME_Standard. The LCME Readiness Room can generate a one-click DCI evidence package showing which lectures cover which standards with what confidence. Medical schools currently spend months manually gathering this evidence for site visits. Journey OS generates it in seconds. This is a category-defining value proposition for the compliance-obsessed medical education administrator.
COVERS_LCME_DOMAIN edges · LCMEContentDomain · LCME_Standard · ADDRESSES_STANDARD edges · LCMEDomainClassifier in P1 Step 04
Moat 07 — Living Student Mastery Model
Not a score — a continuously updated knowledge map
BKT updates in real-time on every attempt. Pimsleur decay models forgetting over time. IRT provides item-level difficulty calibration. The result is a living model: p_mastery = 0.73 today doesn't mean 0.73 tomorrow if the student hasn't reviewed in 30 days. The StudyQueue recommendation algorithm surfaces the items with highest information value at the moment the student is most likely to have forgotten them. Competitors offer quiz scores and percentile ranks. Journey OS offers a continuous, personalized, clinically-weighted map of what each student knows right now — and will schedule the right review before they forget.
BKT 4-parameter model · Pimsleur decay (2.5%/day) · IRT 3PL information function · clinical_consequence_score priority ordering · spaced_retrieval_v1 algorithm
Moat 08 — M1–M4 Longitudinal Continuity
The only platform that spans entire medical school
Most competitors own one segment: pre-clerkship (UWorld for self-study, ExamMaster for faculty), or clerkship (NBME Customized Assessment), or residency (ACGME milestones). Journey OS spans all four years on a single traversable graph. An M3 clerkship item can be EXPLAINS_SAME_CONCEPT linked to an M1 basic science chunk. A student's BKT mastery from Cardiovascular in M1 informs their clinical clerkship readiness assessment in M3. The longitudinal graph is a data asset that no competitor can replicate quickly — it requires years of continuous use to build the prerequisite chain, mastery trajectory data, and cross-year concept linkages that make the Wisdom layer possible.
EXPLAINS_SAME_CONCEPT cross-lecture · PREREQUISITE_FOR edges · WisdomPath trajectory · BKT history across semesters · EPA entrustment tied to mastery + clinical experience
V / Architecture Philosophy

The reasoning your team needs to internalize — not just the decisions

Every major architectural decision has a reason. When your team encounters the temptation to deviate from these, understanding the original reasoning is the best defense against drift.

Why Neo4j + Supabase, not one system
The query shapes are fundamentally different

Coverage heatmap: traverse 18 USMLE_System → ~100 USMLE_Topic → ~400 USMLE_Subtopic → SubConcepts → ContentChunks → Lectures → CatalogCourses — all in one Cypher pattern. This is a 7-hop traversal. In PostgreSQL: a 6-table JOIN that requires materialized views to be performant, loses the ability to query ad-hoc relationship paths, and breaks entirely when you want to add a new edge type. In Neo4j: a single MATCH statement. But pgvector, RLS, JSONB, and auth are PostgreSQL's strengths. The dual-store pattern pays for itself in the first week of query writing.

Why Inngest, not cron jobs or Kafka
Human approval gates require durable execution

step.waitForEvent() for 7 days (faculty review) or 30 days (item approval) is architecturally trivial in Inngest — one line of code. In Lambda + SQS: you need a separate state machine, a checkpoint database, a poll loop, and careful timeout handling. Kafka was considered for the event bus but removed: MSM doesn't need Kafka's throughput (1,000+ events/second). Inngest handles the actual scale (10 concurrent lectures, 3 concurrent generation batches, 100 concurrent BKT updates) with observable, retryable, step-level execution that makes debugging production failures possible.

Why Sonnet + Haiku routing, not one model
$0.12/item target requires model-task matching

Sonnet for core generation and critique: clinical reasoning, multi-step judgment, NBME format evaluation. $0.027/item for two Sonnet calls. Haiku for everything else: classification tasks, distractor writing, rationale, QA scoring, LOD briefs, HyDE vignettes. $0.093/item for three Haiku calls. Total: $0.12/item. Opus for all calls: $0.45/item — 3.75× over budget. A single model for all tasks either over-spends on simple tasks (Sonnet for distractor writing) or under-performs on complex ones (Haiku for clinical reasoning). Model routing is a cost discipline, not a capability compromise.

Why LOD briefs are pre-computed, not live
Context assembly latency: 4,000ms → 450ms

Without pre-computed LOD briefs, P3 context assembly requires: (1) UMLS API call for concept definition (~800ms), (2) Hetionet traversal for drugs/genes (~600ms), (3) MeSH lookup (~400ms). Total: ~1,800ms of synchronous API calls per item, before even calling Claude. With pre-computed lod_briefs in Supabase: single key lookup in ~5ms. For a 30-item batch: the difference is 90 seconds of API latency vs. 150ms. The trade-off is LOD brief staleness (addressed by 180-day expiry and quarterly regen) for a 600× improvement in context assembly speed.

Why FERPA at the database level, not application level
The only guarantee that survives future bugs

Application-level access control means every new route, every future developer, every code change must remember to add WHERE student_id = auth.uid(). One forgotten filter = FERPA breach. PostgreSQL Row-Level Security enforces the policy at the database engine: even if application code is entirely wrong, the database refuses to return rows that violate the policy. This is why "FERPA-first" is an architecture decision, not a feature. The RLS policy is the last line of defense that doesn't depend on any developer doing the right thing.

Why evidence grades on every edge
Path confidence enables the Wisdom layer

Without evidence grades, all edges are equal. With evidence grades (A=1.00, B=0.82, C=0.65, D=0.45), path confidence is the product of edge weights along any chain. An item backed by grade-A TEACHES → grade-B ALIGNS_TO has path confidence 0.82. The WisdomPath algorithm can surface curriculum recommendations based on chains of evidence — "this lecture improves coverage of concepts that are on 6 high-consequence items, via 3 grade-A TEACHES edges." Without evidence grades, this is just a graph traversal that returns irrelevant results. With them, it's a weighted evidence reasoning system.

V-B / Architecture Standards

What makes Journey OS different from a typical Next.js app — and why it matters for hiring and onboarding

Journey OS is not a CRUD app with a medical theme. It spans a knowledge graph, three AI pipelines, a real-time exam engine, a living mastery model, and an LCME compliance chain — across four user personas, nine epics, and 80+ stories. The architecture decisions below exist to make it possible for a 4-person team to ship this without the system becoming unmaintainable. Every engineer on this project must internalize these decisions before writing a line of code.

The core principle

Each thing does one thing and knows only what it needs to know. A database atom knows about Tailwind classes. A service knows about business rules. A repository knows about data access. A route handler knows about HTTP. No level imports from a level above it. No component does more than one job. This discipline is what keeps 9 epics from tangling into each other.

The five architectural layers every engineer works in

LayerLocationKnows aboutDoesn't know aboutTest approach
Atomsshared/components/ui/atoms/Tailwind, Radix, accessibilityDomain, hooks, servicesStorybook / static props
Moleculesshared/components/ui/molecules/
features/*/components/molecules/		Atoms + domain value typesHooks, services, repositoriesStatic domain-typed props
Organismsfeatures/*/components/Molecules, atoms, hooks, domain typesOther features' internalsHook mocked, static organism props
Servicesfeatures/*/services/Domain entities, repositories, eventsReact, HTTP, SQLRepository mocked
Repositoriesfeatures/*/repositories/Generated Supabase types, Neo4j wrapperBusiness logic, ReactIntegration test vs local DB

Atomic Design — 5 levels, hard dependency rule

Atoms
Button, Badge, Input, Spinner, Icon, Label

Zero domain imports. Pure Tailwind + Radix. Reusable outside this project entirely. Any engineer can write these in Week 1 without reading the production bible.

Molecules
BloomBadge, EvidenceGradeIndicator, QaScoreMeter, ClinicalConfidenceBadge, UsmleSystemChip, PipelineStatusBadge

Compositions of atoms with domain-typed props. BloomBadge accepts BloomLevelCode. EvidenceGradeIndicator accepts an EvidenceGrade value object. No hooks. No services. Test with static domain data.

Organisms
ItemCard, CoverageHeatmapGrid, SubConceptReviewCard, ExamTimerBar, MasteryRadarChart, ApprovalQueueTable

Feature UI sections. Use molecules + atoms. Can use hooks for local UI state. Follow Container/Presenter split: organism = presenter, receives data as props. Container wraps it, provides data.

Templates
FacultyLayout, StudentExamLayout, AdminDashboardLayout

Structural shells with named content slots. No data fetching. Accept organisms as children or named props. The exam layout defines the fixed header + question area + nav panel structure.

Pages
Next.js app/*/page.tsx — under 30 lines

Reads route params, passes to container organisms, wraps in a template. No business logic. No data fetching. A page that grows beyond 30 lines has logic that belongs in a container or service.

The Rule
Dependencies flow DOWN only

Atoms → nothing. Molecules → atoms. Organisms → molecules + atoms. Templates → nothing domain-specific. Pages → templates + organisms. Features never import each other's internals — only public index.ts APIs. ESLint enforces this in CI.

Feature-slice directory — not layer-based

Each feature is a vertical slice: components, hooks, services, repositories, types, and tests all live inside one directory. features/item-generation/ contains everything needed to generate, review, and approve assessment items. Changing the generation flow means touching one directory, not eight.

The shared/ directory earns its place by requiring code to be used by 3+ features before moving there. The domain/ directory contains domain entities, value objects, and domain errors — entirely independent of React, Next.js, or Supabase.

features/
  lecture-ingestion/   ← vertical slice
    components/       ← organisms only
    hooks/            ← controllers
    services/         ← use cases
    repositories/     ← data access
    types.ts          ← feature types
    index.ts          ← public API only
shared/components/
  ui/atoms/           ← zero domain
  ui/molecules/       ← domain-typed
  layouts/            ← templates
domain/
  entities/           ← rich models
  value-objects/      ← EvidenceGrade etc
  errors/             ← typed domain errors

Data layer contract — type-safe from schema to UI

The Supabase schema is the source of truth for TypeScript types. After every migration, run pnpm db:types to regenerate database.generated.ts. Every repository, service, and component that touches data uses these generated types — never hand-written interfaces. When the schema changes, TypeScript catches every broken call site automatically.

The typed client pattern
createServerClient vs createBrowserClient

createServerClient() uses the service_role key and bypasses RLS — only in API routes and React Server Components, never in browser code. createBrowserClient() uses the anon key and is fully RLS-enforced — for client components and the student exam UI. Wrong choice = either security hole (service_role in browser) or unnecessary auth friction (anon key in server).

Transaction boundaries
RPC for multi-table atomic operations

Sequential .insert() calls are NOT atomic. If the first succeeds and the second fails, you get partial state. Exam session creation (sessions + session_items) must be atomic — use supabase.rpc('create_exam_session') which wraps both inserts in a Postgres transaction. Any operation touching 2+ tables uses RPC. One-table operations use direct client calls.

Dual-write pattern
Supabase first, Neo4j second, never block on Neo4j

Every write to the knowledge graph follows: (1) Insert to Supabase with neo4j_sync_status: 'pending'. (2) Write to Neo4j. (3) Update sync status to 'synced' or 'failed' on catch. Neo4j failures never throw — they mark sync status and the weekly reconciliation job retries. This is enforced by the BaseRepository class.

RLS is the floor
Application-level filters are extra, not sufficient

Row-Level Security policies on every user table are the authoritative access control — not WHERE institution_id = ? in application code. Application filters can be bypassed by bugs. RLS cannot. For FERPA compliance, this distinction matters: student data is inaccessible via RLS regardless of application logic. If it's not in RLS, it's not a security control.

OOP for domain, functions for utilities

Journey OS uses OOP where it adds value: domain entities (AssessmentItem, SubConcept, ExamSession) are classes with behavior that enforces invariants. Value objects (EvidenceGrade, QAScore, BloomLevel) are immutable classes validated at construction. The three-hub invariant is enforced in AssessmentItem.fromGeneration() — it's impossible to construct an item without all three hub connections. Utilities (RRF scoring, path confidence, Pimsleur decay) are pure functions.

VII / Team Structure

What roles you need and what skills matter most

Full-Stack Engineer · 2 roles
Core product builders

Strong in Next.js App Router, TypeScript, Supabase. Can build both UI and API routes. One focuses on faculty-facing features (upload, review, generation, blueprint). One focuses on student-facing features (exam mode, mastery dashboard, practice). Both need comfort with Cypher for KG query work.

Backend/Pipeline Engineer · 1 role
Pipeline + graph specialist

Deep in Inngest, Neo4j, Python sidecars. Owns P1, P2, P3 pipeline functions. Comfortable with NLP tooling (MetaMap, UMLS API). Writes and optimizes Cypher. Sets up MedCPT + pptx-renderer sidecars. Handles weekly crons and reconciliation. Should have previous experience with ETL pipelines or data engineering.

AI/ML Engineer · 1 role
Generation quality + measurement

Owns prompt engineering for all Claude calls. Maintains evaluation harness (RAG eval, prompt regression tests). Implements BKT update + IRT calibration logic. Handles HyDE retrieval optimization. At T4: GNN training, Louvain community detection. Should understand psychometrics at least conceptually — these algorithms are grounded in measurement science.

Medical Education Advisor · 1 role
Domain expertise (part-time)

Not an engineer. A faculty member or curriculum specialist who can validate: are generated items clinically accurate? Are TaskShell templates pedagogically sound? Is the Physician Task → Question Type mapping correct? Reviews the misconception categories against real student errors. Doesn't need to write code. Needs 4-8 hours/week during development. Critical for clinical confidence tier peer review.

Critical skills across all engineers

  • Cypher fluency — the coverage heatmap, StudyQueue, and ECD queries are all complex Cypher. Everyone writes graph queries.
  • Inngest patterns — step.run(), step.waitForEvent(), step.sendEvent(), onFailure. The pipeline architecture depends on understanding durable execution.
  • Supabase RLS — every table change requires a RLS policy decision. FERPA compliance depends on every engineer understanding this.
  • Evidence grades — all engineers must understand A/B/C/D grades and evidence_weight. These are used everywhere; getting them wrong silently corrupts coverage calculations.
  • Dual-write discipline — Supabase first, Neo4j second, always. Neo4j failures never block the user. neo4j_sync_status columns on every relevant table.
  • Three-hub invariant — every AssessmentItem must connect SubConcept + SLO + USMLE_Subtopic before entering the practice pool. This check should be in the post-approval step.
  • safeJsonParse everywhere — never raw JSON.parse on Claude responses. This is a team-wide convention enforced by linting.
  • neo4jQuery wrapper — never raw neo4j-driver. The ESLint rule catches violations at commit time. The wrapper is not optional.

Per-item generation cost breakdown
$0.12/item — fully loaded

2× Sonnet calls (core + critique): ~$0.037. 3× Haiku calls (HyDE + distractors + rationale+QA): ~$0.007. Embeddings: ~$0.0002. LOD brief (amortized from P2): ~$0.0002. Overhead + retries (×1.5): ~$0.067 total. 30-item faculty batch: ~$3.60. A medical school writing 100 exams/year × 40 items/exam = 4,000 items/year = ~$480/year in generation costs. That's ~$12/exam for the entire item generation cost — less than a faculty member's hourly rate for writing one item manually.

Cost controls built in
Three-layer generation rate limiting

C10 resolution: (1) 3 concurrent P3 runs max per faculty, (2) confirmation required for >10 items with cost estimate displayed, (3) 100 items/day/faculty cap in generation_daily_usage. Plus: monthly budget alert at 80% of institution limit via institution_generation_limits table. The budget ceiling is configurable per institution — an institution can set $200/month as their cap and receive Slack alerts at $160.

IX / Risk Matrix

What could hurt the project — and the specific mitigation for each

C
Faculty adoption friction — "I don't trust AI-generated questions"
Medical faculty are deeply skeptical of AI content. If the first batch of generated items has clinical errors, adoption stalls permanently. The critique gate and QA scoring are good but not perfect.
Mitigation: Start with a "showcase" faculty member who has high tolerance for imperfect AI output. Emphasize: AI drafts, faculty decides. Every item requires faculty approval. The component-targeted editor makes refining easier than rewriting from scratch. Clinical confidence tier (H11) gives faculty language to explain review depth to colleagues.
C
UMLS API rate limits during P2 enrichment surge
If 10 faculty upload lectures simultaneously and all fan-out to P2, the 20 req/sec UMLS throttle will cause P2 to run for hours. Faculty won't see LOD enrichment results and may think the system is broken.
Mitigation: Inngest throttle for P2 (20 UMLS req/sec) is already configured. P2 is background/non-blocking — faculty don't need to wait for it. UI clearly labels P2 as "enriching in background" vs. P1 "processing." Consider self-hosting UMLS full release in Supabase for T2+ to remove API dependency entirely.
C
MSM IT delays SAML/SSO configuration
Real faculty and students use institutional SSO. Magic links work for testing but faculty expect to log in with their MSM credentials. IT approval processes at medical schools are notoriously slow.
Mitigation: Start SAML configuration request in Week 1. Run in parallel with development — doesn't block MVP. Use magic links for the first demo cohort. Have a clear fallback plan (institutional email + magic link) in writing before the first real faculty invite.
H
DrugBank license takes longer than expected
DrugBank academic license typically takes 2-3 days but can take 2 weeks if the institution review team is slow. Without it, pharmacology SubConcept enrichment is incomplete and drug mechanism items will be lower quality.
Mitigation: Apply in Week 1 as a parallel action. P1 and P2 work without DrugBank (fall back to UMLS drug data). Flag pharmacology SubConcepts as "partial enrichment" until DrugBank is seeded. No critical path block — but note to faculty that pharmacology items may be lower quality in the first 2 weeks.
H
MetaMap Java service is fragile in containerized environments
MetaMap's Java server has known issues with Docker networking, memory management, and cold starts. Medical NLP setup is the most painful part of the build based on prior experience.
Mitigation: Allocate 2 days in Week 1 specifically for MetaMap setup. Use the medcat-service Docker image as an alternative (Python-based, better containerized). For early development: use UMLS API direct with simple keyword matching as a temporary NER fallback — switch to MetaMap before production. Have a fully documented "MetaMap works on this exact Docker image" reference before scaling the team.
H
Generated item clinical quality insufficient for summative exams
The critique gate catches format issues well. It does not catch subtle clinical errors — inverted causality, outdated dosing, wrong drug class for a specific patient profile. Faculty may approve items that contain errors they didn't catch in batch review.
Mitigation: Clinical confidence tier (H11) — high-consequence items require peer review before entering summative exams. Limit summative exam use to items that are 'peer_reviewed' until the second semester when faculty are more calibrated on item quality. Medical education advisor reviews the first 100 items from each course for patterns. Set expectation: Journey OS is for formative assessment quality in Year 1; summative quality requires 1-2 semesters of calibration.
M
Neo4j Aura outage during exam delivery
AuraDB has a 99.9% SLA but outages happen. Student exam delivery doesn't need Neo4j — items are in Supabase. But the attempt recording and BKT update calls will timeout.
Mitigation: Graceful degradation pattern (neo4jQuery wrapper with fallback values). Attempt recording goes to Supabase immediately (source of truth). BKT update is queued in Inngest and retried when Neo4j recovers. Students see a "mastery updating..." message rather than an error. Exam delivery is never blocked by Neo4j availability.
X / Metrics That Matter

How you'll know if it's working — the numbers that tell the truth

Pipeline Health
≤5 min
P1 SLA for a 60-slide PPTX. Alert if any lecture stays in 'parsing' >10 minutes. This is the first metric faculty will notice.
Item Cost
$0.12
Target cost per complete NBME vignette. If rolling average >$0.20, audit model routing — Sonnet is being used where Haiku should be.
Faculty Approval Rate
≥75%
Percent of generated items approved without major edits. Below 60% means the generation quality or context quality is insufficient. Diagnose by checking critique severity distribution.
QA Score (avg)
≥0.75
Average QA score across approved items. Items scoring 0.65-0.75 are borderline — review the distractor homogeneity and lead-in type components specifically.
Coverage Velocity
+2%/week
Increase in confirmed CoverageRecord count per course per week. Tracks whether generation is keeping pace with curriculum upload. Plateau = faculty bottleneck in review pipeline.
Mastery Growth
+0.05/week
Average p_mastery increase per student per week of active use. Below 0.03 = either items are too hard (check p-values), items are too few (check coverage), or students aren't practicing (check session frequency).
BKT Update Lag
≤2 sec
Time from attempt submission to mastery dashboard update. This is the real-time feel of the platform. Degrade >5 seconds = investigate Inngest queue depth or Neo4j write latency.
Dead Letter Rate
≤1%
Percent of pipeline runs ending in dead letter queue. >2% = systematic failure in one pipeline step. Diagnose by checking pipeline_dead_letters.step_name distribution.
